Open VSX Removes 77 Malicious Evil Twin Extensions Exfiltrating Developer Data

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 14 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A cluster of 77 extensions on the Open VSX marketplace has been found to impersonate legitimate developer tools while transmitting information about the systems and development environments on which they were installed. The "evil twin" extensions were uploaded to the repository between July 26 and August 1, 2026, according to Manifold Security. The packages have been removed from Open VSX as of

Open VSX evil-twin extension exfiltrating developer data to mangorbit.com AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound connections from code editors / Node extension hosts to the mangorbit.com exfiltration infrastructure used by all 77 malicious Open VSX 'evil twin' extensions. The domain is a hard IOC registered 11 days before the campaign and confirmed as the single collection endpoint for every package. Rationale: mangorbit.com (and its pulse/api/cb subdomains) is stated in the article as the single exfil endpoint for all 77 packages, registered 15 Jul 2026 — a hard, campaign-specific IOC with effectively zero legitimate use.
ATT&CKT1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / sandbox detonating one of the sample extensions for analysis
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving the IOC domain
  • Proxy/DLP appliance pre-fetching flagged URLs for categorization
  • Blocklist-testing automation confirming the domain is sinkholed
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe") // exclude analyst manual IOC checks
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host + local user, confirm the initiating process is a code editor/extension host (Code.exe, Cursor, node) and enumerate installed Open VSX extensions against the 19 named IDs. 2) Contain: block mangorbit.com and all subdomains at the proxy/DNS, isolate the endpoint if a recon-variant extension is present, and force-remove the offending extension. 3) Hunt: pull DeviceNetworkEvents/DnsEvents for the fallback subdomains and check other developer endpoints for the same extension IDs or first-seen resolution of mangorbit.com.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "mangorbit.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationHostName has "mangorbit.com" or RequestURL has "mangorbit.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationPort, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DNS TXT fallback-channel lookup to mangorbit.com (recon-variant contingency) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the article's stated contingency mechanism: the malicious code queries a DNS TXT record under mangorbit.com to retrieve a fallback exfiltration URL if the primary domain is blocked. TXT queries to this domain are a distinct, high-fidelity signal separate from ordinary A-record egress. Rationale: The article explicitly describes a DNS TXT fallback-URL retrieval mechanism under the primary domain — TXT queries to mangorbit.com are behaviorally distinct from A-record exfil and near-uniquely tied to this campaign's contingency logic.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1008
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate DNS diagnostic tools (dig/nslookup) run by an analyst against the IOC
  • Recursive resolver caching/propagating a TXT lookup for enrichment
  • Threat-intel platform actively probing the domain's DNS records
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the client host issuing the TXT query and check whether an evil-twin extension is installed; TXT to this domain implies the primary A-record channel was already blocked. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block all mangorbit.com records at the resolver and isolate the endpoint. 3) Hunt: extract any URL returned in DNS TXT responses and add it to blocklists; sweep for those secondary hosts across the fleet.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "mangorbit.com"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("pulse.mangorbit.com","pulse2.mangorbit.com","api.mangorbit.com","cb.mangorbit.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "mangorbit.com"
| where QueryType == "TXT" or QueryTypeName == "TXT"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, QueryTypeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChainDrop / Mini Shai-Hulud npm preinstall hook downloading standalone Bun runtime AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the ChainDrop worm's execution pattern: an npm preinstall lifecycle hook that downloads a standalone Bun runtime to execute a bundled second-stage payload. Detects node/npm spawning a bun binary from a package-install context — a technique Socket flagged as new for this Shai-Hulud variant. Rationale: Socket/Microsoft describe ChainDrop as delivering a Bun-based payload via an npm preinstall lifecycle hook that downloads a standalone Bun runtime — node/npm→bun with a preinstall context is a specific, rarely-benign chain.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately using Bun as a package manager/runtime in their toolchain
  • CI pipelines that install Bun via a postinstall/preinstall step intentionally
  • Monorepo build scripts that orchestrate bun from node
  • Bun self-update spawned by an existing bun process
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("run build","run dev","run test") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "node_modules\\.bin")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the parent npm command line and the package being installed; confirm whether Bun is a sanctioned tool for this developer/repo. 2) Contain: kill the bun process tree, quarantine the downloaded runtime binary (hash it), and revoke the developer's npm and GitHub tokens (worm steals and reuses npm tokens). 3) Hunt: search for the three campaign SHA256 hashes, .npmrc token access, and outbound connections to npm-cache.com across all developer hosts and CI runners.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.cmd","npm","cmd.exe","bash","sh")
     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "preinstall"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bun.exe","bun") or TargetProcessName has_any ("bun.exe","bun")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node","npm","cmd.exe","bash","sh") or ParentProcessCommandLine has "preinstall"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: npm preinstall Hook Spawning Bun Runtime (ChainDrop / Mini Shai-Hulud)

Mini Shai-Hulud persistence via .claude and .vscode config injection AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the ChainDrop worm planting autostart hooks by injecting Claude and Visual Studio Code configuration files into cloned repositories, creating a developer-to-developer and AI-coding-agent infection path. Detects node/bun/git writing config files under .claude or .vscode directories. Rationale: Microsoft/Socket state the worm injects Claude and VS Code config files and plants autostart hooks in .claude and .vscode to reach developers and AI coding agents — config writes to those specific dirs by node/bun/git is the concrete persistence artifact.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately editing .vscode/settings.json or extensions.json via the editor
  • Dotfile-management tooling (chezmoi, git) syncing .claude/.vscode across machines
  • A repo checkout that legitimately ships committed .vscode workspace config
  • VS Code / Claude extension itself rewriting its own settings on update
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe") // exclude the editor itself writing its own settings
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the written config file against the repo's committed version and inspect for injected autostart commands, MCP server entries, or recommended-extension pointers to the evil-twin IDs. 2) Contain: revert/remove the injected config, revoke the developer's GitHub credentials (worm uses stolen GitHub creds to push these), and scan the repo history for the injection commit. 3) Hunt: check other clones/forks of the repo and downstream developer machines for the same config artifacts and for bun-runtime execution.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.claude\", @"\.vscode\")
| where FileName in~ ("settings.json","extensions.json","mcp.json","config.json","CLAUDE.md")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","bun.exe","git.exe","npm.cmd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.claude\", @"\.vscode\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("settings.json","extensions.json","mcp.json","config.json","CLAUDE.md")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","bun.exe","git.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Mini Shai-Hulud Persistence via .claude/.vscode Config Injection

ChainDrop stealer egress to npm-cache.com C2 / delivery channel AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to npm-cache.com, the ChainDrop campaign's typosquatted secondary domain used alongside GitHub-based delivery to distribute the Mini Shai-Hulud stealer. Distinct network pivot from the Open VSX mangorbit infrastructure, targeting the npm-worm side of the article. Rationale: npm-cache.com is a pre-extracted campaign IOC typosquatting npm's cache infrastructure; contact from a developer/CI host is high-fidelity for the ChainDrop domain-based delivery channel described by Socket.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer misconfiguring npm registry/cache to a typosquatted mirror by accident
  • Security researcher resolving the IOC for analysis
  • Proxy/DLP pre-fetching the flagged domain for categorization
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and the process resolving npm-cache.com; confirm it is a developer workstation or CI runner and whether ChainDrop packages were installed. 2) Contain: block npm-cache.com at DNS/proxy, isolate the host, and rotate npm + GitHub tokens on that account. 3) Hunt: correlate with npm preinstall→bun execution and .claude/.vscode injection on the same host, and sweep CI logs for the 450 affected packages / 2,244 artifacts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "npm-cache.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "npm-cache.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ChainDrop Stealer Egress to npm-cache.com

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] KEV exposure hunt — Langflow, Tomcat, N-central and knaithe campaign CVEs unpatched · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Langflow unauthenticated RCE via /api/v1/auto_login + /api/v1/validate/code (CVE-2026-9198) · [LLM] Langflow (python/uvicorn) process spawning shell interpreter — post-RCE code execution · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Post-RCE persistence written by Langflow python process (cron/systemd/authorized_keys)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Langflow unauthenticated RCE via /api/v1/auto_login + /api/v1/validate/code (CVE-2026-9198) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the two Langflow API endpoints that CVE-2026-9198 chains: /api/v1/auto_login (mints a SUPERUSER token for any unauthenticated caller) and /api/v1/validate/code (executes attacker-supplied Python via exec()). This is the exact exploit path documented by SentinelOne/Mallory and the public PoC/Metasploit module, not a generic web-attack template. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable endpoint paths (/api/v1/auto_login and /api/v1/validate/code) confirmed by SentinelOne, BleepingComputer and Mallory for CVE-2026-9198 — these paths are near-zero in benign traffic, making them high-fidelity. Defender AH left empty as it has no inbound web-request telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-9198/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-orders-feds-to-patch-actively-exploited-langflow-rce-flaw/ • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/CVE-2026-9198
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Rapid7) probing the Langflow host for CVE-2026-9198
  • Internal red-team or pentest validating the patch with the public PoC
  • Langflow developers legitimately using the code-validation feature during flow authoring (validate/code from trusted internal IPs)
  • Automated CI health-checks that call auto_login on an internally-managed Langflow instance
Suppression filter
| where not(SourceIP in ("10.0.0.0/8") and RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nessus","qualys","Nuclei"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the SourceIP hitting both endpoints; confirm whether /api/v1/validate/code carried a POST body and returned 200. Check the Langflow version (patched = 1.10.1). 2) Contain: if unpatched and the request succeeded, isolate the Langflow host, block the SourceIP at the WAF, and rotate any secrets accessible to the Langflow service account. 3) Hunt: pivot to endpoint process telemetry on the Langflow host for python/uvicorn spawning shells (UC: Langflow shell spawn) and outbound connections in the minutes after the request.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("/api/v1/validate/code", "/api/v1/auto_login")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceAction, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow (python/uvicorn) process spawning shell interpreter — post-RCE code execution AIExploitation High
Hunts a Langflow worker process (python/python3/uvicorn/gunicorn whose command line references langflow) spawning a shell or command interpreter. CVE-2026-9198's /api/v1/validate/code runs attacker Python via exec(); the observable follow-on is that Python process launching sh/bash/powershell to establish a foothold. Rationale: Grounded in the corroborated exec()-based RCE mechanism of CVE-2026-9198: the Langflow python worker executing a shell child is the highest-fidelity host-side artefact. Falcon/Datadog cannot see the langflow command line cleanly (ProcessRollup2 exposes ParentBaseFileName, not parent cmdline), so those pivots widen to python-parent + shell-child and are hunting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-9198/ • https://mallory.ai/stories/019fc374-6930-78d6-aa9e-b348144b46ef
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Langflow custom component or tool that legitimately shells out (e.g. a flow invoking a CLI utility)
  • Container entrypoint scripts where uvicorn/gunicorn is launched from a bash wrapper (parent/child inverted but noisy)
  • Admin running maintenance scripts inside the Langflow virtualenv
  • pip/package post-install hooks spawning sh during a deploy of the Langflow host
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "pip install" and ProcessCommandLine !has "-m venv"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine — reverse shells, curl|bash, base64 python one-liners, or /dev/tcp redirects are decisive. Correlate timestamp with UC1 web hits from the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the python parent tree, and preserve /proc and command history for the langflow service account. 3) Hunt: search DeviceNetworkEvents from the same InitiatingProcess for outbound connections, and check for persistence writes (cron/systemd/authorized_keys) by the same python process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "langflow"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","pwsh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "langflow"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

KEV exposure hunt — Langflow, Tomcat, N-central and knaithe campaign CVEs unpatched AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces any host in the fleet still exposing the three CVEs CISA added to KEV on 2026-08-05 (Langflow CVE-2026-9198, Tomcat CVE-2026-34486, N-central CVE-2026-18556/18577) plus the perimeter CVEs the knaithe/KnYuan actor used in manual ops (NetScaler CVE-2026-3055, Marimo CVE-2026-39987, IKE VPN CVE-2026-33824). Directly supports the FCEB Aug-7 remediation deadline. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE IDs from the CISA KEV addition and the Unit 42 knaithe campaign (all cross-checked against BleepingComputer/HelpNetSecurity), plus the vendor-stated fixed versions (Langflow 1.10.1; Tomcat 11.0.21/10.1.54/9.0.117), so the RecommendedSecurityUpdate column is directly actionable. Non-endpoint SIEMs left empty — vuln inventory isn't shipped to Datadog/Falcon FDR/CloudWatch. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/08/03/deepseek-ai-autonomous-cyberattacks-hermes-agent/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-orders-feds-to-patch-actively-exploited-langflow-rce-flaw/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Stale TVM inventory reporting a CVE on a host already patched but not yet re-scanned
  • Vulnerable software present but not internet-exposed (lower priority, not a false result)
  • Duplicate device entries after a hostname change inflating the count
  • Third-party appliance where the embedded Tomcat/Langflow version isn't independently patchable
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hits by internet-exposure (IsInternetFacing) and severity; confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is below the fixed version. 2) Contain: for internet-facing Langflow/NetScaler/Tomcat hosts, prioritise emergency patching or WAF virtual-patching ahead of the Aug-7 FCEB deadline; restrict management interfaces. 3) Hunt: for each still-vulnerable host, run UC1/UC2/UC4 against its telemetry to confirm it hasn't already been exploited before you patch.

| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

Post-RCE persistence written by Langflow python process (cron/systemd/authorized_keys) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a Langflow python/uvicorn process (command line references langflow) creating or modifying Linux persistence artefacts — cron entries, systemd units, SSH authorized_keys, or shell rc files. Anticipates the persistence step following the corroborated CVE-2026-9198 exec() RCE, pivoting on file telemetry rather than process telemetry. Rationale: Chains off the corroborated exec()-based Langflow RCE: a python worker writing cron/systemd/authorized_keys is a specific, high-value persistence signal distinct from the process-spawn pivot (UC2). Confidence is Medium because persistence is inferred from the RCE mechanism, not explicitly described in the article; Falcon FileWritten cannot see the langflow cmdline so it widens to python context + persistence path. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-9198/ • https://mallory.ai/stories/019fc374-6930-78d6-aa9e-b348144b46ef
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1543.002 T1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow container init writing systemd/cron units during legitimate deployment or upgrade
  • Config-management tooling (Ansible/Puppet) running under a python interpreter touching /etc/systemd
  • Admin adding an SSH key to the langflow service account for legitimate automation
  • Application logrotate or self-update writing to /etc paths from the python venv
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "ansible" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "pip install"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the written artefact — a new cron/systemd entry invoking curl/bash/nc or an unexpected authorized_keys entry is decisive; correlate with UC1/UC2 hits on the same host. 2) Contain: remove the malicious persistence file, isolate the host, disable and re-key the langflow service account, and revoke any planted SSH keys. 3) Hunt: enumerate all cron/systemd/authorized_keys changes fleet-wide by python processes in the same window, and check outbound connections from any newly-installed unit.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "langflow"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/systemd/system", "/.config/systemd", "/.ssh")
    or FileName in~ ("authorized_keys","crontab",".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "langflow"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/systemd/system", "/.config/systemd", "/.ssh/authorized_keys", "/.bashrc", "/.bash_profile", "/.profile")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

QuickFox Supply Chain Attack Delivers FDMTP Backdoor via Trojanized Windows Installer

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 17 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed what has been described as a "long-standing supply chain attack" on QuickFox, a virtual private network (VPN) and network acceleration tool designed for overseas Chinese users. According to Fortinet FortiGuard Labs, the supply chain attack has been ongoing since at least August 2025 and involves a trojanized version of the application to deliver FDMTP, a

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] tasklist process fingerprinting spawned by QuickFox app (Steam/wallet evasion check)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] QuickFox trojanized installer beacons to look-alike CDN cdns3.51quickfox.cn · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] QuickFox Electron renderer downloads firebase-app-compat.js JS loader · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — QuickFox Supply Chain Attack Delivers FDMTP Backdoor via Trojanized Windows Inst
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] FDMTP DLL side-load: Client.dll / update.bin dropped in user-writable path · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] FDMTP backdoor C2 beacon to icloud-cdn.net · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
QuickFox trojanized installer beacons to look-alike CDN cdns3.51quickfox.cn AIDelivery High
Hunts any endpoint resolving or connecting to the attacker-controlled look-alike domain cdns3.51quickfox.cn, which masquerades as the official QuickFox domain (51quickfox.com) and stages the malicious JS loader and next-stage ZIP. Contact with this host is inherently the supply-chain delivery signal — legitimate QuickFox uses 51quickfox.com. Rationale: cdns3.51quickfox.cn is the article's primary typosquat CDN (vs legit 51quickfox.com) staging firebase-app-compat.js and the FDMTP ZIP; any contact is malicious. Corroborated by FortiGuard PSIRT FG-IR-25-685 (DLL hijacking in QuickFox online installer). Cross-checked against: • https://fortiguard.fortinet.com/psirt/FG-IR-25-685 • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/chinese-apt-campaign-targets-entities-with-updated-fdmtp-backdoor
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1036.005 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / sandbox intentionally detonating the trojanized installer
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment tooling actively resolving the IOC domain
  • DNS sinkhole or protective-DNS logging the query as blocked (still worth reviewing)
  • Internal malware-analysis lab hosts replaying PCAPs
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("malware-lab01","sandbox-detonate")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess that contacted cdns3.51quickfox.cn and the installed QuickFox version (check DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory for QuickFox < 3.59.6, earliest affected 3.0.51.0). 2) Contain: isolate the host, block cdns3.51quickfox.cn and icloud-cdn.net at proxy/DNS, and quarantine any firebase-app-compat.js / ZIP dropped under user-writable paths. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId for tasklist execution, Client.dll/update.bin drops, and side-loaded host processes beaconing to icloud-cdn.net.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "cdns3.51quickfox.cn" or RemoteUrl endswith ".51quickfox.cn"
| where RemoteUrl !has "51quickfox.com"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(), Procs=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName,5) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "cdns3.51quickfox.cn" or DnsQuery endswith ".51quickfox.cn"
| where DnsQuery !has "51quickfox.com"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DnsQuery
| order by LastSeen desc

QuickFox Electron renderer downloads firebase-app-compat.js JS loader AIExploitation High
Hunts the fetch of the trojan's staged JavaScript loader files firebase-app-compat.js (malicious, Firebase-SDK mimic) and firebase-analytics-compat.js from the attacker CDN. This is the article's specific execution pivot where the modified Electron renderer HTML pulls and runs the fingerprinting loader. Rationale: firebase-app-compat.js and firebase-analytics-compat.js are the two named payload filenames staged on cdns3.51quickfox.cn; the malicious one masquerades as the Firebase SDK. Matching filename + typosquat host is near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://fortiguard.fortinet.com/psirt/FG-IR-25-685
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate apps loading genuine Google Firebase compat SDK from firebasejs CDN (excluded by the 51quickfox.cn host filter)
  • Sandbox detonation of the installer
  • Proxy replay / IOC validation traffic
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has "firebasejs" and RemoteUrl !has "gstatic.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the requesting process is the QuickFox/Electron binary and capture the dropped firebase-app-compat.js for reversing. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the CDN, and remove the QuickFox install; flag for reimage if second-stage confirmed. 3) Hunt: search the same host for tasklist fingerprinting, Client.dll/update.bin drops, and icloud-cdn.net beacons.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("firebase-app-compat.js","firebase-analytics-compat.js")
| where RemoteUrl has "51quickfox.cn"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has_any ("firebase-app-compat.js","firebase-analytics-compat.js")
| where Url has "51quickfox.cn"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, HttpUserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

tasklist process fingerprinting spawned by QuickFox app (Steam/wallet evasion check) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts tasklist.exe executed by the QuickFox/Electron process, matching the loader's fingerprinting routine that enumerates running processes to abort on steam.exe (sandbox/gamer evasion) and to require one of 26 target apps (Xshell, Navicat, DBeaver, Exodus, Binance, Ledger Live, Telegram, etc.). Process-enumeration descended from a VPN client is highly anomalous. Rationale: The loader runs tasklist to check for steam.exe and 26 named apps before proceeding; tasklist parented by a VPN accelerator (QuickFox) is behaviourally unique and article-specific. Kept hunting tier because a curious user could run tasklist, though not from QuickFox's tree. Cross-checked against: • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.fdmtp
ATT&CKT1057 T1518.001 T1497.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • QuickFox legitimately shelling out to tasklist for diagnostics (rare — validate against the fixed 3.59.6 build)
  • Endpoint management/inventory agent enumerating processes
  • Support engineer troubleshooting inside the app's install directory
  • Renamed/portable QuickFox build in a non-standard path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductVersion !startswith "3.59"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree — confirm QuickFox spawned tasklist and check the installed version against affected range 3.0.51.0–pre-3.59.6. 2) Contain: isolate host and block the delivery CDNs; snapshot memory before reimage. 3) Hunt: look for the subsequent ZIP download from cdns3.51quickfox.cn and Client.dll/update.bin side-load on the same DeviceId.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "tasklist.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "quickfox" or InitiatingProcessFileName has "quickfox"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "tasklist.exe"
| where ParentProcessName has "quickfox"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FDMTP DLL side-load: Client.dll / update.bin dropped in user-writable path AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the drop and load of the FDMTP side-loading artifacts — Client.dll (Generation 1) and update.bin (Generation 2 encrypted FDMTP loaded by a malicious DLL) — in user-writable directories, launched via DLL side-loading by a signed benign executable. Targets the article's two payload generations. Rationale: Client.dll (Gen1) and update.bin (Gen2 encrypted FDMTP) are the two named side-load artifacts; anchoring on both filenames + a user-writable path + non-system parent narrows the generic Client.dll name to the campaign's drop pattern. FortiGuard PSIRT confirms DLL hijacking in the installer. Cross-checked against: • https://fortiguard.fortinet.com/psirt/FG-IR-25-685 • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/chinese-apt-campaign-targets-entities-with-updated-fdmtp-backdoor
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software updaters writing an unrelated update.bin to AppData/Temp
  • Third-party app shipping its own Client.dll during install
  • Developer build artifacts named Client.dll under a project Downloads/Temp folder
  • Browser cache/temp writes of similarly named files
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "update.bin" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","updater.exe") and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped Client.dll/update.bin, identify the loading (side-loaded) parent binary and verify its signature vs its load path. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the artifacts, and block cdns3.51quickfox.cn / icloud-cdn.net. 3) Hunt: check DeviceImageLoadEvents for Client.dll loaded from the same folder by a signed benign exe, and correlate outbound C2 to icloud-cdn.net.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName in~ ("update.bin","Client.dll")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\Downloads\")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("update.bin","Client.dll")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\Downloads\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FDMTP backdoor C2 beacon to icloud-cdn.net AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections to icloud-cdn.net, the FDMTP command-and-control / defense-evasion domain used by the deployed backdoor to receive GetInfo requests, plugins and commands and to exfiltrate the host survey. Anchors on the second-source-confirmed C2 IOC, surfacing the initiating (side-loaded host) process. Rationale: icloud-cdn.net is the pre-extracted C2/defense-evasion IOC tied to FDMTP beaconing and exfiltration; a typosquat of Apple's iCloud CDN, it has no legitimate enterprise use. Surfacing InitiatingProcessSHA256 exposes the side-loaded host process. Cross-checked against: • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/chinese-apt-campaign-targets-entities-with-updated-fdmtp-backdoor • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.fdmtp
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Typo-driven user browsing to a parked/unrelated icloud-cdn.net page
  • Threat-intel/IOC validation tooling resolving the domain
  • Sandbox detonation traffic
  • Protective-DNS logging the blocked query
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess and its SHA256 — a side-loaded/non-browser process beaconing to icloud-cdn.net is high-confidence FDMTP. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block icloud-cdn.net and cdns3.51quickfox.cn, and kill/quarantine the beaconing binary and its side-loaded Client.dll/update.bin. 3) Hunt: review scheduled task creation and Run-key writes by the same host process (FDMTP plugin persistence) and check for outbound host-survey uploads following a GetInfo exchange.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "icloud-cdn.net" or RemoteUrl endswith ".icloud-cdn.net"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Beacons=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,5) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Beacons desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "icloud-cdn.net"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Beacons=count() by SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DnsQuery
| order by Beacons desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChainDrop supply chain compromise: Anatomy of a self-propagating worm

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-08-04 16 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A credential-stealing worm hidden in more than 400 compromised npm packages automatically spread across software ecosystems by republishing malicious updates. This analysis details the attack chain, affected environments, and practical guidance for detection, hunting, and remediation. The post ChainDrop supply chain compromise: Anatomy of a self-propagating worm appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Known Mini Shai-Hulud file hashes on disk (setup.mjs / Math_*.js)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Bun runtime bundle spawned by setup.mjs loader · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ChainDrop supply chain compromise: Anatomy of a self-propagating worm
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm preinstall 'node setup.mjs' loader execution (Mini Shai-Hulud worm) · [LLM] Worm persistence via .claude / .vscode config injection by node/bun · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Worm C2 / exfiltration to npm-cache.com, pypi-get.com, js-mirror.com · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Worm GitHub fallback exfil artifacts (results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json) · [LLM] Worm cloud/secret-store credential enumeration via CLI tools spawned by node/bun · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
npm preinstall 'node setup.mjs' loader execution (Mini Shai-Hulud worm) AIInstallation High
Hunts the byte-for-byte-identical worm loader launched by the malicious npm preinstall lifecycle hook: node executing setup.mjs from within a freshly-installed package. This is the single most reliable execution fingerprint of the ChainDrop/Mini Shai-Hulud worm across developer workstations and CI runners. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact process shape (node setup.mjs) and Block 1 KQL, scoped to package-manager parentage so it fires on install-time execution. Corroborated by StepSecurity/Datadog which confirm the setup.mjs loader is byte-identical across all affected packages. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/a-mini-shai-hulud-has-appeared • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-is-back-august/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate npm package that genuinely ships a benign file literally named setup.mjs run at install time
  • Internal monorepo tooling that invokes 'node setup.mjs' as a build bootstrap step
  • Developer manually running 'node setup.mjs' in a project unrelated to the worm
  • CI templates that name a setup script setup.mjs by coincidence
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("internal-build", "monorepo-bootstrap"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent chain — confirm the node setup.mjs invocation was spawned by npm/yarn/pnpm during install and inspect the containing node_modules package name and version; compare that version to the registry's legitimate release/commit history. 2) Contain: isolate the workstation/runner, kill node/bun processes, and immediately revoke & rotate every credential reachable from that identity (npm token, GITHUB_TOKEN, AWS keys, kubeconfig, Vault token) from a known-clean host. 3) Hunt: pivot on DeviceId for bun spawns, results-*.json writes, outbound to npm-cache.com, and any npm publish activity indicating onward propagation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(3d)
| where FileName in~ ("node", "node.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm", "npm.cmd", "npm.exe", "node", "node.exe", "yarn", "yarn.exe", "pnpm", "pnpm.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall", "npm install", "npm ci", "lifecycle")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(3d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/node"
| where CommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun runtime bundle spawned by setup.mjs loader AIExploitation High
Hunts the second worm stage: the setup.mjs loader launching the downloaded Bun runtime to execute the heavily-obfuscated ~11MB credential-stealer bundle (Math_Symbol.js) from a bun-dl- staging directory or node_modules. Distinct process-tree pivot (node→bun) that catches the malware even where the setup.mjs cmdline is obscured. Rationale: Uses Block 2 KQL and the corroborated payload names (Bun runtime + Math_Symbol.js, downloaded to a bun-dl- dir). node spawning bun during package install is anomalous for the vast majority of environments; StepSecurity/Datadog confirm Bun 1.3.13 executes Math_Symbol.js. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/a-mini-shai-hulud-has-appeared • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1027 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Teams that legitimately use Bun as their JS runtime and invoke it from node-based tooling
  • Build systems that download Bun into a temp dir as a genuine dependency
  • Developers experimenting with bun on a node project
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bunfig.toml", "bun run dev", "bun test"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the node parent was itself an install-time setup.mjs invocation and inspect the bun target script path (bun-dl-*/Math_Symbol.js is high-confidence malicious). 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate bun/node, and rotate all locally-reachable credentials from a clean environment. 3) Hunt: pivot on DeviceId for outbound npm-cache.com/pypi-get.com/js-mirror.com traffic, results-*.json artifacts, and .claude/.vscode file writes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(3d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node", "node.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "setup.mjs"
| where FileName in~ ("bun", "bun.exe")
| where FolderPath contains "bun-dl-" or ProcessCommandLine has "node_modules" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js", "Math_")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(3d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\bun.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/bun")
| where (ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "/node")
| where CommandLine has_any ("Math_Symbol.js", "bun-dl-", "node_modules")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
