Known Mini Shai-Hulud file hashes on disk (setup.mjs / Math_*.js) AIDelivery Medium
Alerts on the three confirmed worm artifact SHA256 hashes touching disk: the npm-tarball preinstall loader, the .claude/.vscode repository loader, and the Math_*.js stealer. Pure IOC match — highest-confidence, near-zero-FP confirmation that an affected package landed on the host. Rationale: Direct match on the article's IOC table SHA256 values (setup.mjs npm loader, setup.mjs .claude/.vscode loader, Math_*.js). Hash IOCs are the definitive on-host confirmation; 30-day window catches earlier installs before the campaign was public. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-is-back-august/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/a-mini-shai-hulud-has-appeared
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • None expected — SHA256 collision is not realistic; a hit is a true positive by definition
  • A security researcher/analyst intentionally storing the sample for analysis (whitelist known malware-analysis hosts)
  • Backup/EDR quarantine copies of the file re-triggering the file-write event
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName in~ ("MALWARE-ANALYSIS-VM", "SANDBOX-01"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the containing npm package + version and whether lifecycle scripts were enabled during install; treat the host as compromised. 2) Contain: isolate the workstation/runner, quarantine the file, and revoke+rotate every credential accessible to that identity from a clean host. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same hashes, then pivot to node setup.mjs execution, bun spawns, and outbound C2 to confirm whether the payload executed vs. was merely staged.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in~ ("9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668")

Worm C2 / exfiltration to npm-cache.com, pypi-get.com, js-mirror.com AICommand & Control High
Alerts on network connections or DNS lookups to the three confirmed attacker-controlled exfiltration domains, especially initiated by node/bun. This is the primary HTTPS exfil channel the worm uses to ship AES-256-GCM-encrypted stolen credentials before falling back to GitHub. Rationale: Matches the pre-extracted C2 domains (npm-cache.com, pypi-get.com, js-mirror.com); Microsoft's IOC table and StepSecurity/Datadog independently confirm npm-cache.com as the primary HTTPS exfil endpoint. Any resolution of these domains is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/a-mini-shai-hulud-has-appeared • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox appliances that deliberately resolve known-bad domains
  • Security proxy that pre-resolves URLs from quarantined samples
  • A typosquat-blocking tool that queries the domains to confirm they're sinkholed
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("threatintel-fetch.exe", "sandbox-agent.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (node/bun = confirmed worm) and the host/identity; assume credential exposure. 2) Contain: block the three domains at the proxy/DNS sinkhole, isolate the host, and revoke+rotate all reachable credentials from a clean environment. 3) Hunt: if node/bun-initiated, pivot on the host for results-*.json artifacts, GitHub repo-creation activity (fallback channel), and unauthorized npm publish events.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("npm-cache.com", "pypi-get.com", "js-mirror.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("npm-cache.com", "pypi-get.com", "js-mirror.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Worm GitHub fallback exfil artifacts (results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts local creation of the worm's serialized/encrypted exfil files named results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json by node/bun/git — the payload writes these before committing them to an attacker-created public GitHub repo described 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again'. Catches the fallback exfil path when the HTTPS C2 channel is blocked. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact exfil filename convention (results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json) and fallback GitHub channel; Akamai/Unit42 corroborate encrypted results committed under results/ to Dune-named 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again' repos. Scoping the writer to node/bun/git suppresses generic result files. Cross-checked against: • https://www.akamai.com/blog/security-research/mini-shai-hulud-worm-returns-goes-public • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1537
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Test frameworks that emit timestamped results-<n>.json reports (e.g. some CI reporters) — differs from the double-numeric results-<ts>-<counter> shape but could collide
  • Benchmarking tools writing results-<epoch>-<run>.json artifacts
  • Data-pipeline jobs that shard output into numbered results files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("mocha.exe", "jest.exe", "pytest.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the containing directory — an untracked git repo staging results-*.json alongside node_modules/setup.mjs is confirmatory; check for a newly-created public GitHub repo under the developer's PAT with description 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again'. 2) Contain: isolate host, revoke the GitHub PAT and all reachable secrets from a clean host, and request takedown of any attacker repo. 3) Hunt: enumerate GitHub audit logs for repo-create + push events from the identity and pivot to npm publish activity.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^results-\d+-\d+\.json$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node", "node.exe", "bun", "bun.exe", "git", "git.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^results-\d+-\d+\.json$"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node", "bun", "git")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Worm persistence via .claude / .vscode config injection by node/bun AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the worm's developer-to-developer persistence path: node/bun (or git during a worm-driven commit) writing Claude and Visual Studio Code configuration files into .claude/ and .vscode/ directories across repository branches. Excludes the legitimate IDE/agent processes that normally own those folders. Rationale: Anchors on the article's stated persistence technique (injecting Claude and VS Code configuration files into repositories) and constrains the writer to node/bun/git while excluding the IDE/agent binaries that legitimately own those folders, isolating the worm's write pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-is-back-august/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate 'git checkout'/'git merge' that materializes committed .vscode/settings.json from a teammate
  • A node-based scaffolding tool (e.g. a project generator) that writes .vscode/extensions.json
  • Dotfile-sync or workspace-bootstrap scripts run via node
  • A Claude Code CLI wrapper invoked through node writing to .claude/
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("git checkout", "git merge", "git pull", "create-", "scaffold")
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the written .claude/.vscode file against the repo's committed version and prior history — worm-injected config lacking a corresponding legitimate PR/commit is the tell. 2) Contain: revert the injected files, revoke the GitHub PAT that pushed them, and isolate the host if a stealer payload is also present. 3) Hunt: pull GitHub audit logs for cross-branch commits touching .claude/.vscode from the identity and check downstream clones for the same injection.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.claude\", @"\.vscode\", "/.claude/", "/.vscode/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node", "node.exe", "bun", "bun.exe", "git", "git.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe", "cursor.exe", "electron.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.claude\", @"\.vscode\", "/.claude/", "/.vscode/")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node", "bun", "git")
| where ActingProcessName !has "code"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Mini Shai-Hulud .claude/.vscode config injection by node/bun

Worm cloud/secret-store credential enumeration via CLI tools spawned by node/bun AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential-access stage where the Bun stealer shells out to gh, aws, kubectl and vault to validate stolen tokens and enumerate npm/GitHub/AWS/Kubernetes/HashiCorp Vault resources. The node/bun→(gh|aws|kubectl|vault) parent-child relationship is a high-signal pivot distinct from the delivery and C2 detections. Rationale: Grounded in the article's credential-collection stages (shell collector grabs the GitHub CLI token; dedicated collectors authenticate to npm/GitHub/AWS/Kubernetes/HashiCorp Vault to enumerate secrets). The node/bun parent spawning gh/aws/kubectl/vault with auth/enumeration verbs is a behavior legitimate installs almost never exhibit. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/a-mini-shai-hulud-has-appeared
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1526 T1087.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A node-based deploy/CD script that legitimately calls 'aws sts get-caller-identity' or 'kubectl get secrets' as part of a pipeline
  • IaC tooling wrapped in node that runs 'vault kv get' to fetch config
  • A developer CLI (e.g. a custom npm script) that invokes 'gh auth status' to check login state
  • Backstage/Terraform node wrappers enumerating cloud resources
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("deploy", "terraform", "pipeline", "ci-", "backstage")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the node/bun parent traces back to an install-time setup.mjs/Math_Symbol.js chain rather than a known CD job; enumerate which credentials the CLI calls touched. 2) Contain: revoke and rotate every enumerated identity's secrets (npm token, GitHub PAT, AWS keys, kubeconfig, Vault token) from a clean host and isolate the runner. 3) Hunt: correlate to cloud-side logs (CloudTrail sts:GetCallerIdentity / secretsmanager, GitHub audit, Vault audit) for the same identity and to outbound C2 / results-*.json exfil.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node", "node.exe", "bun", "bun.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("gh", "gh.exe", "aws", "aws.exe", "kubectl", "kubectl.exe", "vault", "vault.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("auth token", "auth status", "get-caller-identity", "configure list", "kv get", "get secrets", "read secret", "token lookup")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "/node" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\bun.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "/bun")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\gh.exe", "\\aws.exe", "\\kubectl.exe", "\\vault.exe", "/gh", "/aws", "/kubectl", "/vault")
| where CommandLine has_any ("auth token", "auth status", "get-caller-identity", "configure list", "kv get", "get secrets", "read secret", "token lookup")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Mini Shai-Hulud credential enumeration via gh/aws/kubectl/vault spawned by node/bun

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("npm-cache.com", "pypi-get.com", "js-mirror.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["npm-cache.com", "pypi-get.com", "js-mirror.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    product: windows

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or SHA1 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc") or MD5 in~ ("54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internet-sourced enumeration of TP-Link Omada device-adoption ports (29810-29816) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts external hosts probing an internet-exposed Omada controller's zero-touch-provisioning port range (29810 discovery through 29816 rtty). Forescout found 1,800+ controllers reachable this way; these ports are intended for on-LAN device adoption only, so public-internet volume against them is the serial-number/MAC enumeration step of the ZTP attack chain. Rationale: Pivots on the exact Omada ZTP port range (29810 discovery, 29811 manager.v1, 29812 adopt.v1, 29813 upgrade.v1, 29814 manager.v2, 29815 transfer.v2, 29816 rtty) confirmed against TP-Link's own port FAQ, combined with an external-source predicate — this is the concrete shape of the serial/MAC enumeration Forescout described. Cross-checked TP-Link/Omada advisory and port documentation. Cross-checked against: • https://support.omadanetworks.com/us/bulletin/114950/ • https://support.omadanetworks.com/us/document/13087/ • https://www.tp-link.com/us/support/faq/3281/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/10/tp-link-patches-four-omada-gateway.html
ATT&CKT1595.001 T1595.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internet-wide background scanners (Shodan, Censys, GreyNoise) sweeping the 29810-29816 range against an accidentally-exposed controller
  • A legitimate remote MSP performing bulk device adoption over a site-to-site VPN whose egress IP is not in the RFC1918 exclusion list
  • NAT/CGNAT collapsing many internal adoption sessions behind one public IP, inflating the per-source count
  • Security team's own external vulnerability scanner (Qualys/Nessus/Forescout) profiling the controller
  • Load-balancer or reverse-proxy health checks hitting the management ports
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<known_scanner_ips_ref_table>"]))     // replace with a watchlist(); optional GreyNoise/known-scanner suppression
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the DestinationIP is an Omada controller and whether it is intentionally internet-exposed; check whether the SourceIP is a known scanner (GreyNoise) or a single actor touching multiple adoption ports. 2) Contain: if the controller should not be internet-facing, firewall-block inbound WAN to 29810-29816 (and 8043/8088/8843) immediately and restrict adoption to the management VLAN. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same SourceIP for follow-on allowed connections to the adoption port (see the initial-access UC), and review the controller for any device adopted from an external address or duplicate serial/MAC.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where RemotePort between (29810 .. 29816)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemoteIPType == "Private"
| summarize Conns=count(), DistinctPorts=dcount(RemotePort), DestPorts=make_set(RemotePort), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP
| where Conns > 20     // 20 = enumeration threshold; a legit host adopts a device with a handful of packets, not a sweep
| order by Conns desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DestinationPort between (29810 .. 29816)
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false     // adoption/discovery must originate on-LAN; public source = probing an exposed controller
| summarize Conns=count(), DistinctPorts=dcount(DestinationPort), DestPorts=make_set(DestinationPort), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationIP
| where Conns > 20     // 20 = enumeration threshold vs. background single-packet internet scans
| order by Conns desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort>=29810 RemotePort<=29816
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count(as=connCount))
| connCount > 20

Rogue device adoption from the public internet to Omada controller (default-cred/race exploit) AIExploitation Medium
Detects a successful/allowed inbound connection from a non-RFC1918 source to the Omada adoption ports (29812 adopt.v1 / 29814 manager.v2). Legitimate zero-touch adoption always originates from a managed device on the LAN — an allowed adoption handshake sourced from the internet is the device-spoofing + cloud-adoption race condition that lets an attacker authenticate with default credentials (CVE-2025-9290 / CVE-2025-15544 / CVE-2025-15627). Rationale: Anchors on port 29812 (port.adopt.v1) and 29814 (port.manager.v2) with an allowed action from a public source — the exact network signature of Forescout's spoof-a-pending-device + win-the-adoption-race scenario, which is impossible for a legitimately on-LAN device. Ports verified against TP-Link's Omada SDN port FAQ. Defender/Falcon left empty: the controller is a network appliance, not an EDR-onboarded endpoint, so this inbound-to-appliance flow is only visible to the perimeter firewall. Cross-checked against: • https://support.omadanetworks.com/us/bulletin/114950/ • https://www.tp-link.com/us/support/faq/3281/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-9289/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cloud-based/off-site Omada controller legitimately adopting remote devices over WAN where those devices' public IPs are expected
  • Remote branch device adopting through a controller whose firewall NATs the branch to a public IP not in the RFC1918 list
  • A misconfigured firewall rule that legitimately forwards WAN traffic to adoption ports for a supported remote-adoption deployment
  • Penetration test or Forescout/BAS tooling replaying the adoption exploit against the controller
Suppression filter
| where DestinationIP !in (dynamic(["<sanctioned_wan_adoption_controller_ips>"]))     // optional: exclude controllers with an approved remote-adoption deployment (watchlist)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SourceIP geolocation/ASN and whether any remote-adoption deployment is sanctioned; on the controller, list devices adopted in the alert window and look for a device whose serial/MAC was already present (duplicate/spoof) or that used default credentials. 2) Contain: block inbound WAN to 29812/29814 at the firewall, force-remove the rogue device, and rotate the controller admin password plus any exposed device secrets (cleartext username, MD5 hash, VPN keys). 3) Hunt: from the same SourceIP look for a preceding enumeration burst and subsequent XSS payloads to the admin ports (8043/8088/8843), and audit for newly created VPN tunnels or config pushes.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DestinationPort in (29812, 29814)     // port.adopt.v1 / port.manager.v2 — the device-adoption handshake
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false     // adoption from the internet should never happen; it is a spoofed/rogue device
| where DeviceAction in~ ("allow","allowed","permit","accept","Permit")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where NOT cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) AND NOT cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) AND NOT cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src)

Stored XSS / JavaScript injection into Omada controller admin UI (CVE-2025-9289) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to the Omada controller web-admin ports (8043/8088/8843) carrying JavaScript/HTML injection markers. Maps CVE-2025-9289 and CVE-2025-15628 — the attacker persists script in an admin field so an authenticated administrator's browser executes it and phishes their cloud-controller credentials. Rationale: Combines the Omada web-admin ports (8043/8088/8843, per TP-Link's port FAQ) with common XSS injection tokens to catch the CVE-2025-9289/CVE-2025-15628 admin-UI JavaScript injection Forescout used to phish admin credentials. URL/query-based payloads are captured; note stored-XSS via POST body may be missed if the proxy does not log bodies — pair with the ImWebSession table where request bodies are available. Defender/Falcon empty: web request targets the appliance, not an EDR host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-9289/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-9289 • https://support.omadanetworks.com/us/bulletin/114950/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1189
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security scanner (Burp/ZAP/Qualys) actively testing the controller for XSS with the same payload tokens
  • A legitimate admin pasting configuration text that happens to contain 'onload=' or 'javascript:' into a controller field
  • URL-encoded query strings in normal portal-authentication flows that coincidentally contain matched substrings
  • WAF logging both the request and its own sanitized copy, double-counting the event
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Burp", "Nessus", "Qualys", "OWASP ZAP", "nuclei")     // suppress known security-scanner user-agents
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the RequestMethod/RequestURL contains an actual injection (decode %3Cscript) versus a scanner probe, and identify whether the SourceIP is internal (admin browser) or external; capture the DestinationIP controller. 2) Contain: if a persisted payload is confirmed, restrict admin-UI access to a management VLAN, patch to the fixed Omada firmware, and invalidate admin sessions plus rotate cloud-controller credentials. 3) Hunt: correlate the SourceIP with prior adoption-port activity, and review controller admin fields/objects for stored script and any anomalous outbound POST of admin credentials to attacker infrastructure.
CommonSecurityLog

| where DestinationPort in (8043, 8088, 8843)     // Omada controller web-admin/portal ports
| where RequestURL has_any ("<script", "javascript:", "onerror=", "onload=", "%3Cscript", "document.cookie", "String.fromCharCode")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Greatness phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platform has expanded from credential phishing to adversary-in-the-middle attacks and device-code phishing targeting Microsoft 365 accounts. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Spoofed RingCentral email failing SPF/DMARC/DKIM but delivered to inbox via whitelist · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] OAuth 2.0 device-code authentication flow success (Greatness device-code phishing) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] M365 sign-in from confirmed Greatness AiTM proxy IP 38.248.95.214 · [LLM] Endpoint/mail contact with confirmed Greatness C2 panel.securehubcloud.com or proxy 38.248.95.214 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] M365 token replay: non-interactive sign-in from IP never used interactively by the user · [LLM] Post-compromise Microsoft Graph multi-service enumeration from single session · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Spoofed RingCentral email failing SPF/DMARC/DKIM but delivered to inbox via whitelist AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound mail whose header-From is ringcentral.com yet fails SPF/DMARC and lacks DKIM, but still lands in the inbox — the exact Greatness delivery trick where a whitelisted domain drove SCL -1 despite failed authentication. Article-specific because it anchors on the spoofed service@ringcentral.com sender plus the auth-fail-but-delivered contradiction. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact contradiction: header-From ringcentral.com with SPF/DMARC fail + no DKIM yet DeliveryAction Delivered to Inbox/folder (SCL -1 whitelist bypass). Cross-checked BleepingComputer and The Hacker News writeups. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate RingCentral notifications routed through a new/third-party relay that temporarily breaks SPF alignment
  • Internal mail forwarding/mailing lists that strip DKIM and re-originate RingCentral mail
  • Marketing or transactional sub-senders on RingCentral's behalf not yet in the SPF record
  • Org still running a blanket domain allow-list that intentionally bypasses auth for ringcentral.com
Suppression filter
| where SenderIPv4 !startswith "104.245." // exclude RingCentral-published sending ranges if maintained in a watchlist
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the NetworkMessageId, confirm SenderIPv4 is an IONOS/hosting range unrelated to RingCentral's published sending infra, and check the URL body for a Greatness landing button. 2) Contain: soft-delete/ZAP the message from all recipient inboxes and add a transport rule requiring valid DMARC for ringcentral.com (replace the blanket allow-list). 3) Hunt: pivot on recipients to UrlClickEvents and subsequent Entra sign-ins (see AiTM/token-replay UCs) and sweep other whitelisted trusted domains for the same auth-fail-but-delivered pattern.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain =~ "ringcentral.com" or SenderDisplayName has "ringcentral"
| extend AuthDetails = tolower(tostring(AuthenticationDetails))
| where AuthDetails has "\"spf\":\"fail\"" or AuthDetails has "\"spf\":\"softfail\""
     or AuthDetails has "\"dmarc\":\"fail\"" or AuthDetails has "\"dkim\":\"none\""
| where DeliveryAction == "Delivered" and DeliveryLocation == "Inbox/folder"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderIPv4, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain =~ "ringcentral.com" or SenderDisplayName has "ringcentral"
| extend AuthDetails = tolower(tostring(AuthenticationDetails))
| where AuthDetails has "\"spf\":\"fail\"" or AuthDetails has "\"spf\":\"softfail\""
     or AuthDetails has "\"dmarc\":\"fail\"" or AuthDetails has "\"dkim\":\"none\""
| where DeliveryAction == "Delivered" and DeliveryLocation == "Inbox/folder"
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderIPv4, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails
| order by TimeGenerated desc
M365 sign-in from confirmed Greatness AiTM proxy IP 38.248.95.214 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any successful Entra ID authentication sourced from 38.248.95.214, the IP confirmed by The Hacker News as a live Greatness AiTM proxy replaying MFA-approved M365 tokens against victims for 2+ weeks. Pure IOC hit, high fidelity. Rationale: 38.248.95.214 is corroborated by The Hacker News as an active AiTM proxy IP authenticating against compromised M365 accounts; ErrorCode/ResultType 0 restricts to successful token replay. Direct IOC, minimal FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html
ATT&CKT1557 T1550.001 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher or IR team sandboxing the Greatness kit from the same egress (rare)
  • Threat-intel scanning infrastructure that happens to reuse the netblock after takedown
  • A legitimate user behind an unrelated service NAT if the IP is later reassigned
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify every AccountUpn that authenticated from 38.248.95.214 and the Applications/resources accessed; treat each as compromised. 2) Contain: revoke all refresh and access tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset + re-MFA, and block the IP at Conditional Access / edge. 3) Hunt: for each affected account review OAuth consent grants, inbox rules, and Graph enumeration (see discovery UC), and expand to other hosting/VPN IPs replaying the same user's tokens.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where IPAddress == "38.248.95.214"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, Application, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ConditionalAccessStatus, IsInteractive
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where IPAddress == "38.248.95.214"
| where ResultType == 0
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ConditionalAccessStatus, IsInteractive, Location
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OAuth 2.0 device-code authentication flow success (Greatness device-code phishing) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces successful Entra ID sign-ins that used the OAuth device-code grant — the second Greatness branch that obtains tokens without an MFA prompt on the phishing domain. Device-code auth is rare in most tenants, so successful ones (excluding sanctioned Azure CLI/PowerShell use) are high-value hunting leads. Rationale: Article explicitly names the device-code phishing branch of Greatness; AuthenticationProcessingDetails carrying 'Device Code' isolates OAuth device-grant sign-ins, with sanctioned CLI/PowerShell apps excluded to cut baseline noise. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/greatness-phaas-adds-device-code.html
ATT&CKT1528 T1621
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code login for smart TVs, conference-room devices, or IoT onboarding
  • Developers/admins using device code with custom apps not in the exclusion list
  • Azure CLI/PowerShell device-code auth if run under a renamed app registration
  • Help-desk assisted enrollment flows that legitimately use device code
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "Windows-AzureAD-Authentication-Provider"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user actually initiated a device-code login on a real device; if not, treat as phishing. Check the IPAddress against hosting/VPN ranges and the same user's normal geo. 2) Contain: revoke tokens, reset credentials, and add a Conditional Access policy blocking device-code flow for user populations that don't need it. 3) Hunt: correlate the sign-in time with a preceding RingCentral-spoof email click, and check for subsequent token replay and Graph enumeration from a different IP.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails) has "Device Code"
| where Application !in~ ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell")
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, Application, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, IsInteractive
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails) has "Device Code"
| where AppDisplayName !in~ ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell")
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
